content.p: "Irish mob" is a phrase that gets attached to very different things. In New York it means a small, violent crew that held the rackets of one Manhattan neighbourhood, including its docks. In Montreal it means a mostly Anglo-Irish network whose members stole from trucks, and who were later tied to cocaine trafficking and a huge hashish shipment through the port. In Cleveland it has been used for the men convicted of a paid killing in 1969. In Oklahoma it is the name of a prison gang whose members were convicted of trafficking methamphetamine and other crimes. There was never one organisation behind these cases, and the sources describe no single chain of command linking them. What they share is a label, and in the New York case a working relationship with the larger Italian-American crime families, which the sources describe as both an alliance with the Gambino family and, in the Crime Museum's telling, service as a killer squad for it.
This account takes the cases in turn, using what the court records, newspapers and museum histories say about each, and notes where those sources disagree.

The Westies are a group tied to the phrase "Irish mob" in New York. They operated on the West Side of Manhattan, in the Hell's Kitchen neighbourhood. The Mob Museum says estimates of their size range from 20 to 60 members. In the 1960s, it says, Mickey Spillane (not the author) took control of the neighbourhood's rackets. The rackets, it says, ran from bookmaking and loansharking to a grip on union locals tied to the Garden, the Coliseum and the waterfront.

The Mob Museum dates the change of power to 20 August 1976, when Spillane's main muscle, Eddie Cummiskey, was shot dead at the Sunbrite Bar. James "Jimmy" Coonan, an up-and-comer, was ready to take over, and Spillane began to withdraw from his rackets. Coonan had been working with an established loan shark, Ruby Stein, who also worked with "Fat Tony" Salerno of the Genovese family. He also recruited Mickey Featherstone, whom the museum describes as a violent and emotionally troubled Vietnam War veteran from a working-class Irish-American family in Hell's Kitchen.

According to the Mob Museum, Coonan was also meeting Roy DeMeo, a hitman for the Gambino family, and one of DeMeo's crew, Danny Grillo. It was probably that relationship, the museum says, more than any other, that set Coonan up for success. In May 1977, it says, Coonan orchestrated the deaths of Stein and Spillane. The museum cites the author T.J. English, whose 1990 book The Westies says that DeMeo killed Spillane as a present to Coonan. The deal brought an alliance with the Gambino family in Hell's Kitchen, although some of Coonan's crew were hesitant.

The Crime Museum tells the rise differently and in more lurid detail. It says Coonan was born on 21 December 1946 in Manhattan, the son of an accountant for mobsters, and that when he was 18 his father was kidnapped by Spillane, who was said to have pistol-whipped him. In its account Coonan bought a machine gun and fired a full clip at Spillane's crew, without hitting anyone, and then built the Westies with Featherstone, kidnapping, torturing and murdering members of the Hell's Kitchen crew until Spillane went into hiding. The Mob Museum does not describe any of this, and the two accounts should be read as different tellings of the same rise rather than a single agreed history.

The Crime Museum also says the Westies owed money to Ruby Stein and decided to remove the debt by killing him. Its account is that they dismembered the body and threw the remains into the Hudson River, but that one member forgot to deflate the lungs, so Stein's torso washed ashore and was found a few days later. In 1979, it says, Coonan and Featherstone were arrested for the murder of a bartender, Harold Whitehead, and both were acquitted.

The Westies' reach shows most clearly in a case that has little to do with street violence. The Intrepid Sea, Air and Space Museum, built around a Second World War aircraft carrier moored at Pier 86 on the Hudson, opened on 3 August 1982 inside the Westies' territory. The Mob Museum says members of the gang infiltrated it, siphoned off hundreds of thousands of dollars in ticket sales and put union members in no-show jobs.

The route in was union work. Members of Local 1909 of the International Longshoremen's Association staffed the museum; the union controlled about 30 positions, including ticket sellers, engineers and maintenance staff. Coonan and Featherstone worked with Vinnie Leone, business manager of the local, who was also connected to the Gambino family. In the museum's telling, the arrangement kept the Westies strong during Coonan's and Featherstone's own prison terms in the early 1980s, and both men were behind bars when the Intrepid opened. Leone was found dead in February 1984, and the Westies kept control of the local.

Featherstone's wife, Sissy, was one of the union members working as a ticket seller. According to the Mob Museum she devised a scheme in which she and a few other women saved tickets already sold, resold them and kept the money. Kenny Shannon, described as a Westie allegedly involved in Leone's death, later became the museum's timekeeper, and Sissy Featherstone became a no-show employee. The month the museum opened, Bobby Huggard was given a no-show job at $227 a week as a gift for perjuring himself in a murder trial, the museum says. The museum's executive director, Wayne Schmidt, reported that the combined rackets cost it $100,000 to $120,000 a year.

The skimming surfaced through the museum's finances. The Intrepid filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in July 1985, listing $16.5 million in assets and $28.4 million in debt; the Mob Museum says the bankruptcy had little to do with the Westies' scheme, and that Schmidt blamed poor attendance and weather. In March 1987 five ticket sellers were let go once the box-office skimming was found. Schmidt said those positions had been filled without his input. The Intrepid is still open.

On 26 March 1987, U.S. Attorney Rudolph Giuliani and Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau announced the indictment of ten Westies under the federal racketeering law, RICO. The counts listed eight murders alongside attempted murders, kidnapping, extortion, loansharking, gambling and drug dealing. The Mob Museum says the indictments grew out of a deal with Featherstone, who offered to testify against his crew when facing 25 years in prison, and who may also have been moved by a falling out with Coonan over how he ran the gang.

The Crime Museum gives its own version of the falling out. In its account Featherstone confronted Coonan about the gang's direction, Coonan authorised the killing of a man named Michael Holly while another Westie, Billy Bokun, was dressed as Featherstone, and Featherstone, arrested for the murder, recorded conversations between the Westies and Coonan to clear himself and bring Coonan down. Those details come from a single page, and the Mob Museum does not repeat them.

After four weeks of testimony, the Crime Museum says, Coonan was found guilty of racketeering. Eight other Westies were also convicted, the Mob Museum reports. The sources disagree on the sentence. The Mob Museum, which dates it to 1988, and W42ST both give 75 years; the Crime Museum says 60. The Crime Museum adds that Jimmy McElroy, a top enforcer, also received 60 years and Richard Ritter, a loan shark and drug dealer, 40. Featherstone has been in the Witness Protection Program since turning informant, according to the Mob Museum.

Coonan was still fighting to get out decades later. In July 2025, W42ST reported that a federal appeals court had dismissed his motion for a sentence reduction, ruling that he was ineligible under current sentencing laws. He was 78 and had served 37 years of a 75-year sentence. The Mob Museum gives his mandatory release date as 1 June 2030.

Across the border, the label attaches to the West End Gang. The Globe and Mail, citing a public inquiry, describes it as a mostly Anglo-Irish, loosely structured crime group. The paper's subject is the Matticks family: Richard and Gerald were the most famous of 14 siblings who grew up in Goose Village, a blue-collar enclave of six streets at the foot of the Victoria Bridge, populated mostly by Italian and Irish immigrants and razed by the city in 1964.

Richard Matticks was born on 7 April 1934. He first made the papers in 1957, with a two-year term for stealing merchandise from trucks. The author D'Arcy O'Connor, quoted by the Globe, recorded repeated arrests for theft, assault and possession of stolen goods between 1963 and 1969, usually ending in fines or short jail time, and then 15 charges of truck hijacking, theft and possession of stolen goods against Richard and his brother Gerald in a single month in 1973, again with light sentences.

The Quebec Police Commission's inquiry into organised crime turned to the brothers in 1979. A public inquiry named Richard, Gerald and two other brothers, Fred and Robert, as leaders of a crew that specialised in truck hijackings and bank robberies. Former members testified that the gang stole televisions, liquor and jeans from trailers and warehouses. It had a locksmith, a safecracker and an electronics specialist who could disarm alarms, and once set off makeshift bombs to confuse police during a holdup. The Globe says the inquiry's report had their proceeds laundered by Peter Ryan, whom it identifies as the actual leader of the West End Gang. Ryan shifted the gang toward cocaine trafficking; after he was murdered in 1984, he was succeeded by Allan "The Weasel" Ross, who ended up with three concurrent life terms for drug trafficking after his arrest in Florida.

Police alleged that by the 1990s the brothers were leaders of the gang with a hold on the Port of Montreal, which let them smuggle large drug shipments that were resold to groups able to sell them on the street. At the end of April 1994 a customs agent noticed that some containers aboard the Norwegian-flagged freighter Thor I, sailing from South Africa, were consigned to apparently bogus shipping companies. Police intercepted 26.5 tonnes of hashish on arrival, which they called one of the largest hashish seizures in Canada.

An empty apartment tied to one of the companies held only a telephone. The janitor said a man paid the rent in cash each month and, shown photographs, identified Richard Matticks. An import-export broker, Pierre Friedman, said he had been hired by Gerald, agreed to cooperate, and wore a hidden microphone. According to court testimony, Gerald and Richard handed him $10,000 in cash. The next day the Sûreté du Québec arrested the brothers and announced a major blow against the gang's control of the waterfront.

The case collapsed. The janitor now said he had lied and could no longer identify Richard. The brothers' lawyers, going through the seized documents, noticed what looked like planted, incriminating faxes. The brothers walked free, and, the Globe reports, a judge threw out the case because the provincial police had tampered with evidence. The ensuing uproar led to a public inquiry and an overhaul of the Sûreté du Québec, and the provincial police spent three years in turmoil.

The brothers' later record was mixed. Gerald was convicted over drug dealing with the Hells Angels. Richard, in 1997, admitted selling cocaine to the rival Rock Machine; the Globe notes the two biker groups were then locked in a turf war. Gerald, present at his brother's sentencing, insisted Richard was innocent and told a Gazette reporter, "The only coke my brother touches is Diet Coke." Richard served his full three-year sentence because the parole board found he had made no effort in prison to show he would change. In 2004, police targeted him as a suspected drug kingpin in an operation code-named Relève, according to a 2008 court judgment. He died in a Montreal hospital at 80, a relative told the Globe in January 2015.

The name did not vanish. In February 2017 the National Post reported that Shane "Wheels" Maloney, described as tied to the West End Gang, had pleaded guilty in Montreal to trafficking 25 kilograms of cocaine for a criminal organisation, possessing explosives and three firearms offences. Prosecutors said he controlled a cache found in raids in October 2012 containing 1,475 sticks of dynamite, two pounds of C-4, detonators, remote controls and hundreds of firearms and gun parts, part of the Sûreté du Québec's Project Loquace, an investigation into a ring importing up to 75 kilograms of cocaine a week. More than 100 people were arrested. Prosecution and defence made a joint submission for a ten-year sentence minus time already served.
content.h2: Cleveland: from newsboys to a paid killing
content.p: Cleveland Historical, a local-history site, records Irish names in several chapters of the city's underworld, though not always in organised-crime terms. In the 1913-14 circulation war between the Plain Dealer and the Leader, newsboys and distributors were threatened and beaten. On 21 November 1914 a railroad switchman, Thomas Gibbons, was shot dead on Detroit Avenue. The site notes that one Plain Dealer distributor, William "Scance" Chambers, was believed by some to belong to a west-side Irish street gang. Whether Gibbons was an innocent bystander or a participant depended on which newspaper was read. Harvey Callahan and Frank O'Neill, both Leader employees, were indicted for the killing; after a two-week trial in January 1915 Callahan was acquitted and the charge against O'Neill dropped.

The site also traces Thomas "Black Jack" McGinty, a second-generation Irish-American and former boxer who became a fight promoter and gambling operator. He ran a gambling spot raided by Safety Director Elliot Ness on 21 July 1936, and in 1930 built the Mounds Club on Chardon Road, just over the county line, which it describes as a swanky club with entertainment and gambling. Moe Dalitz and Morris Kleinman, members of what the site calls the Cleveland Gang, were reputed silent owners. Masked gunmen robbed some 300 patrons of an estimated $450,000 there on 29 September 1947, and no one was ever charged. After the state padlocked the club in 1949, McGinty and his associates moved their money to the new Desert Inn in Las Vegas, and in 1951 he was subpoenaed by the Kefauver committee. He avoided prosecution and died in Florida in 1970.

The clearest conviction is the later one. Cleveland.com called Owen and Martin Kilbane "Irish gangsters" convicted of the 1969 contract killing of Marlene Steele, wife of Euclid Municipal Court Judge Robert Steele. The gunman, Richard Robbins, testified that the brothers, known for loansharking, gambling and prostitution, acted on behalf of the judge, who agreed to pay $1,000. Police tied the killing to the judge and the Kilbanes in 1975; all three were convicted at a trial in 1977. In 2018 an appeals court rejected the brothers' bid for a new trial, calling a 37-year delay unreasonable. The brothers had pleaded guilty in 2004 to the 1968 killing of an FBI informant, Andrew Prunella, and have always maintained their innocence in the Steele case.
content.h2: Prison gangs that took the name
content.p: The newest uses of the name describe gangs tied to prisons. In Oklahoma, the Irish Mob Gang, or IMG, grew in the state prison system. KTUL reported in 2016 that it started because some white inmates would not follow the supremacist views of the United Aryan Brotherhood. A Tulsa police gang-unit sergeant told the station it has operated since the 1990s and that its members work with Black and Hispanic gangs outside because it is good for drug business, and that police did not consider it a threat to most people, though it had been linked to four or five murders.

In April 2022 the U.S. Attorney's office for the Western District of Oklahoma announced that a five-year state-wide investigation had produced 125 convictions, including more than a dozen high-ranking incarcerated members. The case relied on a dozen wiretaps, more than half on contraband cell phones smuggled into state prisons. The seizures totalled over 525 pounds of methamphetamine and heroin, 212 guns and nearly $600,000. David Postelle, then 39, whom prosecutors called the gang's head, was held responsible for over 270 kilograms of methamphetamine and received a life sentence; his predecessor, Chad Hudson, received 348 months. The defendants included two state prison guards, and death threats were made against two prosecutors early in the inquiry.

In California, the East Bay Times reported in 2016 that Coby Phillips, then 42, a founding member of the Family Affiliated Irish Mafia, or FAIM, a street gang from the Rodeo and Crockett area that also operates in state prisons, faced a second trial for the 2004 killing of Aryan Brotherhood member Darryl Grockett after a jury deadlocked in 2013. Prosecutors also alleged he put out a hit on a lawyer from jail, a killing they said never took place. His attorney called the allegation a "Hail Mary" and denied that Phillips wrote the note prosecutors cited. These were allegations at the time of the report; the sources opened here do not give the outcome.
